def-fd-x00:
## Definition

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval of time and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open set of Cartesian spatial coordinates $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$, with the standard right-handed orientation. A vector field $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ is in the regularity class used here if $u$, its first time partial derivatives, its first spatial partial derivatives, and its second spatial partial derivatives all exist and are continuous. Scalar fields have the corresponding stated continuous derivatives: a pressure field $p$ has continuous first spatial partial derivatives; a density field $\rho$ has continuous first time and first spatial partial derivatives and takes values in $(0,\infty)$. A scalar function of one or several displayed real variables is $C^1$ when its first partial derivatives exist and are continuous; piecewise-$C^1$ paths have the meaning in the line-integral definition below. For a scalar field $f$, set $\nabla f=(\partial_{x_1}f,\partial_{x_2}f,\partial_{x_3}f)$; for a vector field $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$, set $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}u_j$, $\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_{x_2}u_3-\partial_{x_3}u_2,\partial_{x_3}u_1-\partial_{x_1}u_3,\partial_{x_1}u_2-\partial_{x_2}u_1)$, and $\Delta f=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}^2f$, with $\Delta u$ applied componentwise. Define the row-component Jacobian $D_xu=(\partial_{x_j}u_i)_{i,j}$ and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=\sum_{j=1}^3u_j\partial_{x_j}u$.

For constants $\rho_0>0$ and $\mu>0$, define the kinematic-viscosity parameter $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. The formal constant-density incompressible Navier--Stokes system is

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0.$$

Its associated formal Cauchy stress matrix is $\sigma=-pI_3+\mu(D_xu+(D_xu)^{\mathsf T})$. The corresponding steady Stokes system is $\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0$ together with $\operatorname{div}u=0$; it omits both the time derivative and convective term. These are definitions of pointwise mathematical systems and do not assert that a physical fluid has a solution with the stated regularity.

For a barotropic branch, let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ have two continuous derivatives and let $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ have continuous spatial partial derivatives through order two. The formal compressible Euler system for $u$ and positive density $\rho$ is

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$

At a constant background density $\rho_0>0$ with $P'(\rho_0)>0$, the positive parameter $c$ defined by $c^2=P'(\rho_0)$ is the sound-speed parameter of this mathematical branch. A separate rotating linear system, for constant $\Omega\in\mathbb R^3$ and scalar field $q$, is $\partial_tu+2\Omega\times u=-\nabla q$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$.

The vorticity field is $\operatorname{curl}u$. If $\gamma:[a,b]\to\Omega$ is a closed piecewise-$C^1$ oriented curve, with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$, its circulation is $\oint_\gamma u\cdot d\mathbf r$. If $S$ is a compact oriented regular surface patch in $\Omega$ with unit normal $n_S$, its volume-flux observable is $\int_S u\cdot n_S\,dS$. The traction on $S$ is $\sigma n_S$ and the formal resultant force is the componentwise surface integral $\int_S\sigma n_S\,dS$. For a steady field, a streamline is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to\Omega$ satisfying $x'(s)=u(x(s))$; the parameter $s$ is a curve parameter, not time. A closed material loop on a time interval $J\subseteq I$ is a $C^1$ map $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ with $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$ and $\partial_tX(t,\theta)=u(t,X(t,\theta))$; the definition asserts no existence of such a map. On an exterior domain, $f(x)\to f_\infty$ uniformly in direction as $|x|\to\infty$ means $\sup_{|e|=1}\|f(re)-f_\infty\|_2\to0$ as $r\to\infty$, using absolute value when the field is scalar.

For one optional SI interpretation, the dimensions are $[x]=\mathrm m$, $[t]=\mathrm s$, $[u]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $[\rho]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $[p]=\mathrm{Pa}$, $[\mu]=\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $[\nu]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, $[V]=[q]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, and $[\Omega]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Thus $[\operatorname{curl}u]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, circulation has units $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, volume flux has units $\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}$, stress has units Pa, and resultant force has units N. In this interpretation $\rho_0,\mu,P,V,\Omega$ are inputs to the displayed formulas, while $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$ and $c^2=P'(\rho_0)$ are derived quantities relative to those formulas; this classification is not asserted to be universal across physical theories.
def-fd-real-trigonometric-functions:
## Definition

For $z\in\mathbb C$, let $E(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}z^n/n!$ be the complex exponential and set $s_{\mathbb C}(z)=(E(iz)-E(-iz))/(2i)$ and $c_{\mathbb C}(z)=(E(iz)+E(-iz))/2$, where $i^2=-1$. For $t\in\mathbb R$, define the real-valued functions $S(t)=\operatorname{Re}(s_{\mathbb C}(t))$ and $C(t)=\operatorname{Re}(c_{\mathbb C}(t))$, with $\operatorname{Re}(x+iy)=x$. These are the real restrictions of the complex sine and cosine; on real inputs they agree with the usual real sine and cosine.
lem-fd-x02-vector-triple-product:
## Statement

For all $a,b,c\in\mathbb R^3$, the Euclidean cross product satisfies

$$a\times(b\times c)=b\langle a,c\rangle-c\langle a,b\rangle.$$
lem-fd-x03-tanh-error-bounds:
## Statement

For every real $s\ge0$,

$$0\le s-\tanh s\le \frac{s^3}{3},\qquad 0\le 1-\tanh s\le 2e^{-2s}.$$
thm-fd-x01:
## Statement

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ and $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $\rho_0,\mu,U,L,c>0$, and set $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$, $\operatorname{Re}=UL/\nu$, and $\operatorname{Ma}=U/c$. Define $T=Ut/L$, $X=x/L$, $I^*=\{Ut/L:t\in I\}$, and $\Omega^*=\{x/L:x\in\Omega\}$. For the incompressible branch, let $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ have continuous first time and first and second spatial partial derivatives, and let $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ have continuous first spatial partial derivatives. Write $u^*:I^*\times\Omega^*\to\mathbb R^3$ and $p^*:I^*\times\Omega^*\to\mathbb R$ for the corresponding fields with the same stated regularity. Set $u(t,x)=Uu^*(T,X)$ and $p(t,x)=p_{\mathrm{ref}}+\rho_0U^2p^*(T,X)$, where $p_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is constant. Then the original system is equivalent under this invertible change of variables to

$$\partial_Tu^*+(u^*\cdot\nabla_X)u^*=-\nabla_Xp^*+\operatorname{Re}^{-1}\Delta_Xu^*,\qquad \operatorname{div}_Xu^*=0.$$

For the barotropic branch, let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ have two continuous derivatives with $P'(\rho_0)=c^2>0$. Let $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ have continuous first time and first and second spatial partial derivatives, let $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ have continuous first time and spatial partial derivatives, and let any potential $V$ have continuous spatial partial derivatives through order two. Write $u^*:I^*\times\Omega^*\to\mathbb R^3$, $\rho^*:I^*\times\Omega^*\to(0,\infty)$, and $p^*:I^*\times\Omega^*\to\mathbb R$ for the rescaled fields with the corresponding stated regularity. Set $\rho=\rho_0\rho^*$ and $P(\rho)=P(\rho_0)+\rho_0c^2p^*$; if a potential is present, set $V=U^2V^*$ with $V^*:\Omega^*\to\mathbb R$. Then the exact transformed equations are

$$\partial_T\rho^*+\operatorname{div}_X(\rho^*u^*)=0,\qquad \partial_Tu^*+(u^*\cdot\nabla_X)u^*=-\operatorname{Ma}^{-2}(\rho^*)^{-1}\nabla_Xp^*-\nabla_XV^*.$$

These are coefficient identities under positive changes of scale. They do not assert a limit as either dimensionless ratio tends to zero or infinity, an error estimate, uniqueness, or identical solutions when geometry or rescaled data differ.

In the optional SI interpretation, $[\rho_0]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $[\mu]=\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $[U]=[c]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $[L]=\mathrm m$, and $[\nu]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$; $\operatorname{Re}$ and $\operatorname{Ma}$ are dimensionless.
lem-fd-real-trigonometric-derivatives:
## Statement

For $t\in\mathbb R$, define $S(t)=\operatorname{Re}((E(it)-E(-it))/(2i))$ and $C(t)=\operatorname{Re}((E(it)+E(-it))/2)$, where $E(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}z^n/n!$ and $\operatorname{Re}(x+iy)=x$. Then $S$ and $C$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$ and satisfy $S'(t)=C(t)$ and $C'(t)=-S(t)$ for every real $t$.
thm-fd-x02:
## Statement

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval, let $\rho_0>0$, let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ have two continuous derivatives, and put $\chi=P'(\rho_0)$. Use standard right-handed Cartesian coordinates $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)\in\mathbb R^3$ and their usual gradient and divergence. For real $t$, use the real functions $S(t)=\operatorname{Re}((e^{it}-e^{-it})/(2i))$ and $C(t)=\operatorname{Re}((e^{it}+e^{-it})/2)$, with $e^z=\sum_{n=0}^\infty z^n/n!$ and $\operatorname{Re}(x+iy)=x$. Define the linear acoustic system on $I\times\mathbb R^3$ at the constant rest state by taking the coefficient of $\epsilon$ in the barotropic mass and momentum equations with constant potential, $\rho=\rho_0+\epsilon r$ and $u=\epsilon v$; the resulting equations are $\partial_t r+\rho_0\operatorname{div}v=0$ and $\partial_t v=-(\chi/\rho_0)\nabla r$. The displayed modes have continuous first time and first and second spatial partial derivatives on this domain. This is a first-variation system; no nonlinear approximation error is asserted.

If $\chi>0$, let $c=\sqrt{\chi}>0$. For a nonzero spatial wave vector $k\in\mathbb R^3$, a real density amplitude $A$ with $|A|<\rho_0$, and a real temporal frequency $\omega$, set $\theta=k\cdot x-\omega t$ and

$$r(t,x)=A C(\theta),\qquad v(t,x)=\frac{A\omega}{\rho_0|k|^2}kC(\theta).$$

For $A\ne0$ this mode solves the linear acoustic system exactly if and only if $\omega^2=\chi|k|^2$; when $A=0$ it is the zero solution for every $\omega$. In the optional SI interpretation, $[\rho_0]=[A]=[r]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $[v]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $[\chi]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, $[c]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $[k]=\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, and $[\omega]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. If the mode is read as the density field $\rho_0+r$, the stated bound on $A$ ensures it stays positive.

If $\chi<0$, then for every $k\ne0$ and real $A$, $\lambda=|k|\sqrt{-\chi}>0$ and

$$r(t,x)=Ae^{\lambda t}C(k\cdot x),\qquad v(t,x)=-\frac{\lambda A}{\rho_0|k|^2}k e^{\lambda t}S(k\cdot x)$$

solve the same linear system and give an exponentially growing Fourier mode when $A\ne0$. This is a statement about the linear system, not a claim that a positive full density exists for all times.

For the rotating linear system on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$, let $\Omega\in\mathbb R^3$ be constant and $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$. Set $e=k/|k|$, choose a unit vector $a\perp e$, and put $b=e\times a$, $\alpha=2\Omega\cdot e$, $z(t)=aC(\alpha t)-bS(\alpha t)$, and $\beta(t)=e\cdot(2\Omega\times z(t))$. The proof constructs such a choice of $a$ for every unit $e$. For any real $W$, the fields

$$w(t,x)=Wz(t)C(k\cdot x),\qquad q(t,x)=-\frac{W\beta(t)}{|k|}S(k\cdot x)$$

solve $\partial_tw+2\Omega\times w=-\nabla q$ and $\operatorname{div}w=0$. These rotating fields have continuous first time and first and second spatial partial derivatives. The signed frequency is $\alpha$, so $|\alpha|\le2|\Omega|$; when $\alpha=0$, $z$ is stationary and no division by $\alpha$ is used. In SI units, $[k]=\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, $[\Omega]=[\alpha]=[\beta]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $[W]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and $[q]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$. These are exact finite-mode solutions of the specified linear systems, not nonlinear fluid solutions or turbulence results.
thm-fd-x03:
## Statement

Let $h,g,k>0$, let $a\in\mathbb R$, and set $s=kh$ and $\omega=\sqrt{gk\tanh(s)}$, using the positive square root. Here $h$ is depth, $g$ a constant acceleration parameter, and $k$ a positive horizontal wave number; $s$ is dimensionless and $a$ is a real elevation amplitude. The strict positivity of $\tanh(s)$ for $s>0$ makes $\omega$ well-defined and positive. Let $x,y\in\mathbb R$ be horizontal Cartesian coordinates and $z\in(-h,0)$ the vertical coordinate, positive upward with the flat mean surface at $z=0$ and bottom at $z=-h$; time $t\in\mathbb R$. Write $\theta=kx-\omega t$. A surface elevation is the scalar field $\eta(t,x,y)$, and a velocity potential is a scalar field $\phi(t,x,y,z)$. Define the finite-depth linear potential-wave problem by

$$\Delta\phi=0\quad(-h<z<0),\qquad \phi_z(t,x,y,-h)=0,$$

$$\eta_t(t,x,y)=\phi_z(t,x,y,0),\qquad \phi_t(t,x,y,0)+g\eta(t,x,y)=0,$$

where $\Delta=\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2+\partial_z^2$. Let $S,C$ be the real sine and cosine functions defined on this page. Then

$$\eta(t,x,y)=aC(\theta),\qquad \phi(t,x,y,z)=\frac{ag}{\omega}\frac{\cosh(k(z+h))}{\cosh(kh)}S(\theta)$$

are fields that are $C^2$ in the spatial variables and $C^1$ in time, with the displayed derivatives extending to $z=-h$ and $z=0$, and they satisfy this system exactly. Define the shallow and deep comparison frequencies by $\omega_{\rm sh}=k\sqrt{gh}$ and $\omega_{\rm deep}=\sqrt{gk}$. They obey

$$0\le\frac{\omega_{\rm sh}^2-\omega^2}{\omega_{\rm sh}^2}\le\frac{(kh)^2}{3},\qquad 0\le1-\frac{\omega}{\omega_{\rm sh}}\le\frac{(kh)^2}{3},\qquad 0\le\frac{\omega_{\rm deep}^2-\omega^2}{\omega_{\rm deep}^2}\le2e^{-2kh}.$$

These are exact statements about the displayed linear boundary problem and its dispersion relation. They assert no nonlinear free-surface solution or error bound.

In the optional SI interpretation, $[h]=\mathrm m$, $[g]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, $[k]=\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, $[a]=[\eta]=\mathrm m$, $[\omega]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and $[\phi]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$.
